Am I required to carry it?

Only if your home is in a high-risk zone (A or V) and your mortgage is from a federally regulated lender, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Check your zone on FEMA's flood map.

76.0% of Alabama's NFIP policies are in high-risk zones (not 76.0% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

How much does it cost here?

Typically about $1,140 a year ($95 a month), fees included. Half of homeowners here pay between $890 and $1,470. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

Low end $890 · Typical $1,140 · High end $1,470 · Highest tenth pay $2,145 or more

Coverage in force: $10.3 billion of building and $1.9 billion of contents coverage across all Alabama policies.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Buy it now: most policies start 30 days after you buy, but there's no wait if you buy it with a new or refinanced mortgage.

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood insurance is bought separately, through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Exceptions: no wait if you buy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, or change coverage at renewal; a one-day wait if a map revision puts the property in a high-risk zone and you buy within 13 months of the revision (44 CFR §61.11). NFIP covers up to $250,000 on the building and $100,000 on contents, which is a separate policy. To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. Past aid paid here is in “Did the government pay homeowners after floods?” below.

Source: floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, fema.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Floods here have led to 44,896 NFIP flood claims and $1.2 billion in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2004, 2005 and 2020.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2004 ($358,242,564), 2005 ($296,765,157), 2020 ($133,115,612). Total paid $1,182,375,995: net building + contents payments by year of loss. Claims are matched by the claims dataset's county code, which may not exactly match a policy's property county.

That is 44,896 claims since 1978 against 46,025 policies in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Why do sites quote different averages for Alabama?

Because they measure different things. From the same FEMA records, the typical single-family home pays $1,140 a year, but the average across every policy type is $1,854.

MeasureAmountWhat it counts
Median cost, single-family homes$1,140premium plus fees; the middle policy
Average (mean) cost, single-family homes$1,320pulled up by a few expensive policies
Median premium only, single-family homes$905before the federal fee, reserve fund and surcharge
Average premium only, single-family homes$1,058the figure many sites quote
Median cost, every policy type$1,266adds condos, rentals and businesses
Average cost, every policy type$1,854

Published averages rarely say which of these they are, or which year. All six here come from the NFIP policies in force on July 31, 2026.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

58.0% of bills here can keep rising: they pay less than FEMA's full-risk price. Those prices step up toward full-risk each year, limited by the yearly cap. Median premium $905, full-risk $1,362 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$905
  • Median full-risk premium$1,362
  • Pay below full-risk58.0% of 17,396

Years to the full-risk price: By law most premiums cannot rise more than 18% a year (FloodSmart puts it at 18–25% for most policyholders); the cap usually does not apply to new policies, and fees and surcharges sit outside it. At the 18% cap, a policy at today's median premium ($905) would take at least about 3 annual renewals to reach the median full-risk premium ($1,362). This is the limit on how fast a bill can climb, not a forecast of any one policy.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How often do the same homes flood here?

Some homes here flood again and again: 7,159 flood-damage applications in FEMA's disaster-aid records came from homes that flooded more than once; 140 of those records came from homes hit in four or more.

  • Repeat-flood damage records7,159
  • Records from homes hit four or more times140

One home appears once for each declared disaster that damaged it, so this counts damage events on repeat-flooded homes, not distinct homes (FEMA says these records cannot be totaled by property). Disaster-aid applications since 2002, separate from NFIP insurance claims.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Repetitive-Loss Flood Properties. Data effective FEMA's current list; retrieved October 26, 2026.

Did the government pay homeowners after floods?

Yes, but not much per household: FEMA approved $423.1 million for homeowners here, about $1,230 per registration, against an average paid flood claim of $33,783.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners); FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective owner registrations by disaster; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Reconciliation & data completeness

Our record counts match the API's own totals; FEMA's official policy count is not yet joined for Alabama.

In-force count: 46,025 policy units (from 29,407 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). Count reconciliation (not a snapshot proof): policies: 29,407 of 29,407 fetched; claims: 44,896 of 44,896 fetched.

What this data cannot tell you

  • Your own premium — it depends on elevation, coverage and deductible. We show where existing policies fall.
  • Private (non-NFIP) flood insurance prices.
  • Your address's exact flood zone — use FEMA's Flood Map Service Center.
  • Why any one premium changes — we show the gap to full-risk, not the cause.
  • A year-over-year premium trend — the in-force snapshot holds only current-term policies, so a like-for-like multi-year index isn't possible from this data. A per-effective-year median is shown only where several years of policies exist.
